extracted.intended_audience: authors querying literary agents (aspiring and debut novelists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critique standards for composing concise, effective query letters to literary agents—what to include, what to avoid, and how to structure a submission for fiction (esp. novels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective hook (show the problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: An effective hook gives us a sense of the problem that drives the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid a book-review opening or vague overview. Show a character, an emotional component, and the problem they face (example contrasted: weak ‘There are stories that never get told…’ vs. strong hook showing Alice Andison’s struggle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell who the main character is, what they want, what's in the way, and the stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: After reading the query I should be able to tell you: 1) Who the main character is; 2) What they want; 3) What's getting in the way of getting what they want; 4) What's at stake if they don't get it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four things should be clear without taking notes. Agents read to get story and style quickly—make it obvious and concise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include plot (choices and stakes) even for character-driven books
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot isn't the events of the book. Plot is choices the characters face and what's at stake with those choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You must have plot in a query. Show the choice the protagonist must make and consequences; focus on the start of the story and what drives it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the main protagonist and the story's beginning
rubrics_metrics.description: You have a limited amount of space to engage your reader. Focus on how the story starts. If the story begins with Vittoria, give her more page time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple characters are introduced equally, you lose focus. Lead with the main character (who wants X but is blocked by Y, must choose Z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show connections between characters clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: If characters are three generations or related, make their linkage obvious in the query.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should not guess relationships—state how characters are linked only if it matters to the opening/action you're describing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comps: include 2–3 recent, genre-appropriate titles (use titles, not just authors)
rubrics_metrics.description: You should include 2–3 books that your intended readers will have read and liked. Comps need to be recent (pubbed no earlier than 2019); on your shelf; and pubbed by a trade house (not self-pubbed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use titles, not an author-only comp. Don't use nonfiction as a comp for a novel. Avoid very old comps (e.g., 2017 may be too old). Avoid using Stephen King as a comp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query word count guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Word count is a flexible target: you can be over 250 without auto-pass; under 250 risks not getting enough story; over 400 is when to sharpen the scissors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A common working target is ~250–300 words. Use as much as you need to get the story on the page, but keep it concise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of technical details and personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Put the word count and category at the close of the query. Personalization and comps should go at the end as well—not at the top.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't lead with category, word count, or personalization; frontload story and hook instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't state the obvious (manuscript complete, 'this is my first novel')
rubrics_metrics.description: You don't need to say it's complete (that's assumed), and agents don't need to know how long you've loved to write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit status statements and self-effacing or needy language; focus space on story and pertinent bio details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bio: brief, relevant, and non-needy
rubrics_metrics.description: The bio is about you, not your work; a couple of lines about where you live/pets/etc. is useful. Avoid long bios and statements that read as needy or naive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have publishing credits include them; otherwise a short personable bio is sufficient—do not spend most of your word count on bio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-writing and excess detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Early drafts are almost always too long. Pare out everything you don't need; too much detail or abstraction stymies agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short sentences are preferable in queries. Remove excess modifiers and tangents; leave only what advances the reader's understanding of the main character, problem, choices, and stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of language and sentence structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use razor-sharp, precise sentences. Avoid burying the subject in clauses and overly long sentences (example: a 35-word sentence is too long for a query).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start sentences with the subject, pluck unnecessary modifiers, and keep sentences digestible for fast reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don't tell
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid telling the reader interpretive statements; instead show the driving events and emotions. 'You're telling, not showing' is a frequent critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace phrases like 'takes us out of the narrative' or 'portrays the sarcastic, yet vulnerable' with crisp scenes or actions that demonstrate tone/character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid internal-conflict-only descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal conflicts in a query are a huge red flag; they suggest the plot may not hold together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Queries should present external problems and stakes or clear choices, not just internal emotional states without action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre labeling: be accurate and useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the most solid description you can (e.g., 'fantasy'), not unhelpful labels like 'new adult' or 'fiction novel.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you call a book a thriller it should have thriller elements (e.g., a ticking clock). Mislabeling invites passes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichés and stock phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'heart of gold' or overused descriptors make a manuscript feel unoriginal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents look for fresh and new—use specific, distinctive language and avoid tired adjectives and metaphors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recent and trade-published comps (no self-pub comps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comps must be on your shelf and trade published; don't use self-published works as comps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also avoid comps older than about 5 years (author suggests no earlier than 2019). Choose comps that illuminate tone/market placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep antagonist and stakes clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Queries must make clear who/what the antagonist is and what the conflict/stakes are (e.g., is the antagonist a machine or a person?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague abstractions like 'alter the human condition' need concrete specifics in a query to be compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid awkward or unclear phrasing that creates misreading
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'a slave-mining operation captures Nik' can be misread; revise for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read for possible misinterpretations and rewrite (e.g., 'a mining operation that uses slaves to dig' instead of 'slave-mining operation').

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and category expectations for YA and MG
rubrics_metrics.description: Queries should match the tone and stakes expected for their category—YA needs edge and a sense of navigating the larger world; otherwise it may read MG.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If querying YA, ensure protagonist faces real-world navigation/coming-of-age stakes and enough story/edge on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't be a supplicant in closing
rubrics_metrics.description: You are not a supplicant; thank the agent for their time and consideration with one closing only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid phrasing that sounds desperate ('I'm looking to team up with an agent to navigate the ropes'); keep closing professional and concise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization: be specific but not frontloaded
rubrics_metrics.description: Personalization is useful but should not lead the query; place personalization later and make it specific to the agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A throwaway or generic personalization is worse than none; include genuine, brief personalization in the closing area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using author-only comps or iconic outliers
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't comp to an author alone (e.g., 'Stephen King'); some authors are in a category by themselves and not useful comps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use titles that signal tone and market rather than relying on an author's name as shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queries should demonstrate what makes the book fresh
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents see familiar concepts often—your query must show the fresh take or distinctive approach that elevates the idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't state 'my book is different'; demonstrate it through specific character details, stakes, voice, or unusual premise hooks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trim bios and avoid irrelevant personal history
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents don't generally care about a writer’s lifelong love of writing or processes—the bio should not consume most of the query.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only include relevant, marketable, or personable facts; omit process anecdotes and obvious assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete specifics instead of abstract statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract phrases like 'alter the human condition' or 'developed abilities' are too vague for a query.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give concrete examples of what the invention/ability/incident does and how it affects character choices and stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing and grammar matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Small grammar or word-choice errors (e.g., 'hid' vs 'hidden') can 'fell your query' and become stumbling blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If grammar and syntax aren't your forte, invest in copyediting or a trusted reader to remove errors before querying.
